text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) establishes a comprehensive framework for the conservation of species that are threatened or endangered, along with the ecosystems upon which they depend. A central legal implication of the ESA is the requirement imposed on federal agencies under Section 7. This provision mandates that any federal agency must ensure that any action they authorize, fund, or carry out is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any species listed as endangered or threatened, nor is it likely to destroy or adversely modify designated critical habitat.

To comply with this requirement, federal agencies are generally required to engage in formal consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Marine Fisheries Service if their actions may affect listed species or critical habitat. The legal implications are significant: if an agency determines that its action is likely to jeopardize a listed species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat, the action cannot proceed unless a specific exemption is granted or the action is modified to avoid the adverse effects. This creates a strong legal barrier against federal projects that would harm biodiversity, placing a high burden on agencies to conduct thorough biological assessments and ensure that their activities do not contribute to the extinction of protected species.
